questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST accurate reason why testing is necessary?
options: It removes every defect from the software so that nothing remains to fail after release
It reduces the risk of poor quality by finding defects and giving stakeholders information
It proves that the software will behave correctly for all users in production use
It makes reviews and static analysis unnecessary because dynamic tests cover the same ground
questions.explanation: Testing cannot guarantee defect-free software or eliminate all risk; its purpose is to reduce the risk of quality-related problems by finding defects and providing information to stakeholders.

questions.question: What is the key difference between error, defect, and failure?
options: A failure produces a defect in the code, and that defect then leads to a human error
A human error can introduce a defect, and executing that defect may cause a failure
The three terms are synonyms and may be used interchangeably in a defect report
A defect can be found by static testing, whereas a failure can be observed by dynamic testing alone
questions.explanation: A human error (mistake) can introduce a defect (fault/bug) into a work product; when the code containing a defect is executed, it may cause a failure (an observable deviation from expected behavior).

questions.question: Which statement about the seven testing principles is CORRECT?
options: Exhaustive testing becomes achievable once a sufficiently large set of test cases is written
The pesticide paradox says that rerunning identical tests raises their defect-finding power over time
Early testing has little effect on cost because defects cost the same to fix at any stage
Testing can reveal defects but cannot prove that none remain
questions.explanation: One of the seven testing principles states that testing can show defects are present, but cannot prove there are no defects remaining, even if none are found.

questions.question: The 'pesticide paradox' principle of testing states that:
options: Repeated identical tests stop finding new defects, so tests need regular review
Test environments gradually degrade in quality and must be rebuilt periodically
Automated tests are exempt from this effect because scripts run identically each time
Testers should retire each test case after one execution to keep the suite fresh
questions.explanation: The pesticide paradox principle notes that repeating identical tests will eventually stop finding new defects, so test cases need to be regularly reviewed, varied, and updated.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes a test case?
options: A document describing the scope, approach, resources and schedule of testing for a whole project
A tool that executes regression tests automatically and stores their outcomes for later analysis
Preconditions, inputs, actions, expected results and postconditions for a test condition
A record of a failure seen during test execution, handed to the developers for investigation
questions.explanation: A test case is a formal specification including preconditions, inputs/actions, expected results, and postconditions, developed to exercise a specific test condition.

questions.question: Which activity is generally considered part of the 'test analysis' stage of the fundamental test process?
options: Running prepared test cases and recording the results against expected outcomes
Examining the test basis to identify features and define test conditions
Preparing the test environment and loading the data needed for execution
Summarizing the results of testing for stakeholders at the end of the test effort
questions.explanation: Test analysis involves analyzing the test basis to identify testable features and define associated test conditions, answering 'what to test'.

questions.question: During which fundamental test process activity are test cases and test procedures created from test conditions?
options: Test monitoring and control
Test design
Test completion
Test implementation
questions.explanation: Test design is the activity where test conditions are transformed into test cases and other testware, answering 'how to test'.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical task performed by a tester rather than a test manager?
options: Defining the overall test strategy and test policy for the whole project
Analyzing and assessing requirements and design specifications for testability
Allocating budget and staff to the planned test activities
Choosing the degree of test automation to adopt across the organization
questions.explanation: Reviewing and analyzing requirements/design specifications, designing tests, and executing them are typical tester tasks, while strategy, resourcing, and automation policy are typically test management tasks.

questions.question: Why is it important to consider the required skill set and mindset when staffing test activities?
options: Testing calls for a destructive attitude in which testers assume developers are careless
Testing is best left to developers, who know the code and the design intent well
Curiosity, critical thinking and attention to detail, plus domain and technical skills
Testing relies on technical skill, so communication abilities matter little for testers
questions.explanation: Effective testing benefits from testers having a critical, curious, attention-to-detail mindset alongside relevant technical and domain knowledge, plus good communication skills.

questions.question: In an iterative software development lifecycle, when should test activities ideally start?
options: Once a complete working system has been integrated at the end of the project
As early as practical, alongside the related development work in each iteration
Only in the last iteration, when the final feature set is stable enough to test
After deployment, so that real user behaviour guides what gets tested
questions.explanation: Regardless of the lifecycle model, test activities should start as early as possible, often in parallel with corresponding development activities (shift-left testing).

questions.question: What characterizes a 'test level' in the context of the SDLC?
options: A classification of defects according to the degree of harm they could cause users
A count of the test cases that were run during one single execution cycle
A group of test activities organized and managed together, sharing a test basis
Another name for a test technique, such as boundary value analysis
questions.explanation: A test level is a group of test activities organized and managed together (e.g., component, integration, system, acceptance testing), each with its own test basis and test objects.

questions.question: Which test level primarily focuses on verifying the interactions and interfaces between integrated components or systems?
options: Integration testing
Component testing
Acceptance testing
System testing of a single isolated component
questions.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interactions and interfaces between components (component integration testing) or between systems (system integration testing).

questions.question: Acceptance testing is typically performed to:
options: Uncovering as many coding defects as possible in individual components
Building confidence that the system meets user, business or regulatory needs
Measuring how much of the source code unit tests have exercised
Standing in for system testing when the schedule is tight
questions.explanation: Acceptance testing is often the responsibility of customers/users or operators and focuses on establishing confidence in the system rather than primarily finding defects.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a functional test type?
options: Measuring the average response time of a search under a heavy user load
Checking that login accepts valid credentials and rejects invalid ones
Reviewing source code for compliance with the team's coding standards
Checking that the application installs correctly on each supported platform
questions.explanation: Functional testing evaluates functions that the system should perform, such as verifying that login authentication behaves correctly for given inputs.

questions.question: Non-functional testing evaluates characteristics such as:
options: Usability, performance efficiency, reliability and security of the system
Whether a business rule yields the correct result for given inputs
Whether the code contains statements that can never be executed
Whether the requirements document is complete and consistently worded
questions.explanation: Non-functional testing evaluates quality characteristics such as usability, performance efficiency, reliability, security, compatibility, and portability.

questions.question: White-box testing is best described as testing that is:
options: Based on the specification alone, with no regard for how the software is built
Based on analysis of the internal structure of the test object, such as its code
Carried out by end users on the live system once it has been released
Focused on quality characteristics such as performance rather than on functions
questions.explanation: White-box testing is derived from and exercises the internal structure or implementation (e.g., code, architecture) of the test object, e.g., using statement or branch coverage.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of confirmation testing (re-testing)?
options: Checking that unrelated parts of the system are unaffected by a change
Measuring system performance under peak load conditions
Checking that a defect reported earlier has been fixed
Validating compliance with applicable security regulations
questions.explanation: Confirmation testing (re-testing) re-executes a previously failed test case to confirm that the reported defect has been fixed.

questions.question: Regression testing is performed to:
options: Checking that changes have not harmed functionality that previously worked
Finding defects in functionality that never existed before the change
Taking the place of confirmation testing once a fix is delivered
Running once at the end of a project as a final sign-off activity
questions.explanation: Regression testing checks that previously working functionality still works correctly after changes (e.g., defect fixes, enhancements, environment changes).

questions.question: In maintenance testing, 'impact analysis' is primarily used to:
options: Assessing the effects of a change on the existing system, intended or not
Estimating how much a new test tool will cost within the testing budget
Choosing which testers should be assigned to the maintenance project
Working out how many test cases exhaustive testing of the system would need
questions.explanation: Impact analysis assesses the changes made to a system for their consequences, helping identify the extent of regression testing needed in maintenance testing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic of static testing?
options: It needs the software under test to be running in a test environment
It applies to source code but cannot be used on requirements documents
It depends on specialized test automation tools in every case
It examines work products such as requirements or code without running them
questions.explanation: Static testing examines a work product (e.g., requirements, design, code, test cases) manually or with tool support, without executing the code.

questions.question: Which of the following defects is MOST likely to be found through static testing rather than dynamic testing?
options: A memory leak that appears only after 48 hours of continuous running
Slow response times when many users are active at the same moment
A race condition that surfaces only under particular timing in production
An ambiguous or missing requirement in a specification
questions.explanation: Static testing techniques like reviews are effective at finding defects in requirements and design documents, such as ambiguities, before any code is executed.

questions.question: In a formal review process, what is the primary purpose of the 'kick-off' activity?
options: Correcting every defect that the reviewers have identified in the work product
Producing the final review report together with the metrics that were collected
Handing out the work product and making sure participants grasp the objectives
Formally closing the review and archiving the reviewed work product afterwards
questions.explanation: The kick-off activity gathers participants, distributes documents, and explains the objectives and process of the review, ensuring everyone understands their roles.

questions.question: Which review type is generally the MOST formal, typically led by a trained moderator and includes defined roles and entry/exit criteria?
options: Informal review
Walkthrough
Technical review
Inspection
questions.explanation: Inspections are the most formal review type, following a defined process with a trained moderator, defined roles, metrics collection, and entry/exit criteria.

questions.question: In a formal review, which role collates the anomalies raised by reviewers and records defects, decisions and open points during the review meeting?
options: Manager
Author
Scribe (recorder)
Moderator (facilitator)
questions.explanation: The scribe (recorder) collects and documents the issues, defects, risks, and open points identified during the review meeting.

questions.question: Which factor is MOST likely to contribute to a successful review process within an organization?
options: Skipping reviewer training to keep review costs low
Holding authors personally accountable when many defects are found
Management support that provides adequate time and resources for reviews
Leaving out follow-up once the defects have been logged
questions.explanation: Success factors for reviews include management support, sufficient time allocated, a blame-free atmosphere, and appropriate training of participants.

questions.question: Black-box test techniques are primarily based on:
options: Analysis of the test object's specification, not its internal structure
Analysis of the internal code structure and control flow of the test object under test
The experience and intuition of the tester, applied without any formal model or document
The programming language and framework in which the system has been implemented
questions.explanation: Black-box techniques derive test conditions and cases from an analysis of the test basis (e.g., specifications) without considering the internal structure of the software.

questions.question: A field accepts integer values from 1 to 100 inclusive. Using boundary value analysis (two-point boundaries), which set of values covers all boundary test points for this range?
questions.explanation: Two-point boundary value analysis tests the minimum and maximum valid boundaries plus the immediately invalid values just outside them: 0 (just below min), 1 (min), 100 (max), and 101 (just above max).

questions.question: A system classifies applicant ages into: 'Minor' (0-17), 'Adult' (18-64), and 'Senior' (65+). How many equivalence partitions exist for valid age values, and how many are needed as a minimum to achieve equivalence partitioning coverage?
options: 3 partitions; at least 3 test cases, one per partition
1 partition; a single test case is enough
3 partitions; exactly 6 test cases are required, two per partition
2 partitions; 2 test cases, one for minors and one for adults and seniors
questions.explanation: There are three valid partitions (Minor, Adult, Senior). To achieve minimum equivalence partitioning coverage, at least one test case per partition is required, i.e., a minimum of 3 test cases.

questions.question: A decision table has conditions C1 and C2, each with true/false values, producing 4 rules. What level of test coverage is achieved if one test case is designed for EACH rule (column) in the table?
options: 100% decision table coverage
0% decision table coverage
50% decision table coverage
Coverage cannot be measured for decision tables
questions.explanation: Decision table coverage is calculated as the number of rules tested divided by the total number of rules. Testing all 4 rules (one test case per rule) achieves 100% decision table coverage.

questions.question: State transition testing is MOST appropriate for testing a system where:
options: Output depends solely on the current input, whatever happened in the past in the system
The software has no distinguishable states, so its behavior cannot be modelled in this way
Behavior depends on the current state and earlier events, within a finite set of states
Only performance characteristics such as throughput and latency need to be checked
questions.explanation: State transition testing is used for systems that can be modeled as a finite number of states with transitions between them, where behavior depends on current state and history (e.g., a login lockout mechanism).

questions.question: Statement coverage measures:
options: The percentage of decision outcomes exercised by the test suite
The percentage of executable statements exercised by the test suite
The percentage of requirements that have at least one test case
The percentage of equivalence partitions exercised by the test suite
questions.explanation: Statement coverage measures the percentage of executable statements that have been exercised by a test suite, a white-box (structure-based) coverage criterion.

questions.question: Consider: IF (a > 0 AND b > 0) THEN ... Achieving 100% decision (branch) coverage for this single decision requires a MINIMUM of:
options: 1 test case, because a single IF has only one branch
2 test cases: one making the decision true and one making it false
4 test cases, covering every combination of the two conditions
One test case per statement contained in the code
questions.explanation: Decision coverage requires each decision outcome (true and false) to be exercised at least once, which for a single IF statement requires a minimum of 2 test cases, regardless of how many conditions make up the decision.

questions.question: Exploratory testing is BEST described as an approach where:
options: Test cases are fully scripted and formally approved before any execution is allowed to begin
Tools generate and execute every test with no involvement from a tester in the process
Testers design, run and learn from tests at once, using findings to steer further testing
Testing is restricted to unit level and is carried out by the developers who wrote the code
questions.explanation: Exploratory testing is an experience-based technique where testers dynamically design and execute tests based on their knowledge and the information they gain during testing, informing further test design.

questions.question: Checklist-based testing relies on:
options: A formal model of valid and invalid input partitions
A mathematical coverage criterion applied to the source code
Test scripts generated automatically from the requirements
A tester's experience and a list of items that guide design and execution
questions.explanation: Checklist-based testing is an experience-based technique where testers design and execute tests to cover items in a checklist derived from experience, standards, or known issues.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical purpose of a test plan?
options: Describing the scope, objectives, approach, resources and schedule of test activities
Recording each defect that has been found so far in the current release of the product
Taking the place of the organization's overall test strategy for all of its projects
Specifying in detail how the system under test is to be implemented in program code
questions.explanation: A test plan describes the scope, approach, objectives, resources, and schedule of intended test activities, and identifies test items, features to be tested, tasks, and risks, among other things.

questions.question: A product risk in software testing is BEST described as a risk related to:
options: The management and control of the test project itself, such as staffing or schedule slippage
Friction between departments in the organization that slows down decision making on the project
The quality of the test object, such as software failing to perform a required function
The licensing costs of the test tools that the team intends to use on the project
questions.explanation: Product risks are directly related to the test object (the quality of the product), such as the possibility that the software might fail to perform its intended functions correctly.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a PROJECT risk rather than a product risk?
options: The application may respond too slowly when many users are active at the same moment
The login function may wrongly accept an incorrect password from an attacker
A key tester may leave before test execution ends, delaying the schedule
The system may be open to SQL injection attacks through its search field
questions.explanation: Project risks relate to the management and control of the test project, such as staffing, skills, organizational, or scheduling issues, whereas the remaining scenarios describe product quality risks.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of tracking entry and exit criteria during test execution?
options: Selecting the programming language that will be used to write the automation scripts
Working out how much each member of the test team should be paid this quarter
Removing the need to produce a test summary report at the end of the testing
Deciding when a test activity can start and when it can be treated as finished
questions.explanation: Entry criteria define the preconditions for starting a test activity, while exit criteria define what must be satisfied to consider the test activity complete; both help manage and control testing.

questions.question: Which of the following fields is typically found in a defect report?
options: The tester's performance rating from the latest appraisal
Unique ID, failure description, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual result, severity
Marketing material from the vendor of the test tool
The complete source code of the application under test
questions.explanation: A defect report typically includes a unique ID, a description of the failure, steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, severity, priority, and status, among other fields.

questions.question: What is a potential RISK of introducing a new test tool into an organization without proper evaluation?
options: The tool corrects the defects it finds without any developer needing to get involved
Unrealistic expectations, underestimated maintenance effort and over-reliance
Tool use removes the testing costs immediately after the purchase has been completed
Introducing a test tool carries no meaningful risk to the project's schedule or budget
questions.explanation: Risks of tool introduction include unrealistic expectations, underestimating time/cost/effort for tool maintenance, over-reliance on the tool, and neglecting to properly evaluate the tool before adoption.

questions.question: Which of the following is a category of test tool support specifically for test execution and logging?
options: Test execution tools that run tests and record the results
Requirements management tools that store and trace requirements
Source code editors used by developers
Project scheduling tools used for planning
questions.explanation: Test execution tools automatically run tests, compare actual and expected results, and log the outcomes, distinguishing them from other categories like requirements or management tools.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why testing contributes to quality assurance?
options: Testing is the same thing as quality assurance and so makes quality assurance redundant
Testing starts only after all of the quality assurance activities have come to an end
Testing and quality assurance are unrelated activities with no information shared between them
Testing is one quality activity among several and supplies information for improvement
questions.explanation: Testing is a quality control activity that gives stakeholders objective information; quality assurance is broader and focuses on process improvement, and test results feed into it.

questions.question: Which statement about the relationship between testing and debugging is CORRECT?
options: Debugging is a testing activity that testers carry out in order to find new defects
Testing and debugging are a single activity, normally performed by the same person
Testing reveals failures; debugging finds and fixes the cause
Debugging takes place before testing in every software development lifecycle model
questions.explanation: Testing can show that failures occur, but locating the underlying defect and fixing it (debugging) is typically a development activity distinct from testing.

questions.question: A tester enters a valid date but the system rejects it due to a coding mistake in the date-validation logic. What is the CORRECT terminology for this coding mistake itself?
options: A defect (fault)
A failure
An error (mistake)
A risk
questions.explanation: The flawed code is the defect (or fault); the human mistake that introduced it is the error, and the observable incorrect behavior when executed is the failure.

questions.question: Which of the seven testing principles states that defects tend to cluster in a small number of modules?
options: Absence-of-errors fallacy
Testing is context dependent
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Defect clustering
questions.explanation: Defect clustering observes that a small number of modules usually contain most of the defects found, or are responsible for most operational failures, similar to the Pareto principle.

questions.question: The 'absence-of-errors fallacy' testing principle warns that:
options: A system with no known defects can safely be considered ready for release to users
Fixing defects has little value if the system still fails to meet user needs
Software with zero defects cannot exist, so searching for them is not worthwhile
Defects tend to appear in the same few modules each time a release is tested
questions.explanation: Even a defect-free system can fail to meet user needs, be unusable, or not fulfill business requirements, so simply removing defects is not sufficient for success.

questions.question: Which testing principle states that testing activities should vary based on the application domain, e.g. a safety-critical system is tested differently from an e-commerce site?
options: Testing shows the presence of defects
Early testing saves time and money
Pesticide paradox
Testing is context dependent
questions.explanation: The 'testing is context dependent' principle recognizes that the extent, techniques, and rigor of testing should be tailored to the specific context, such as safety-criticality, regulations, or risk.

questions.question: Why might independent testers (e.g. a separate test team) find different defects than the developers who wrote the code?
options: Independent testers know the requirements less well, so they test more broadly
Independent testers are barred from talking to developers
Independence ensures that every defect in the product will be found
Independence reduces author bias and brings a fresh perspective on the work
questions.explanation: A degree of independence often helps testers identify defects that authors miss due to their familiarity with and assumptions about their own work, though full independence is not always feasible or desirable.

questions.question: In the context of testing terminology, a 'test condition' is:
options: A testable aspect of a component or system, such as a function, used to base tests on
A specific input value that is used within one single test case during test execution
The final pass or fail status of a test case once the test has been run to completion
The physical or virtual environment in which the planned tests are going to be run
questions.explanation: A test condition is a testable aspect (e.g., a function, transaction, or non-functional attribute) identified from the test basis, from which test cases are later derived.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes 'test basis'?
options: The hardware and infrastructure on which the planned tests are going to be run
The report that summarizes the test results for the stakeholders at the end of testing
Information used as the reference for test analysis and design, such as requirements
The tool used to manage the test cases and track their execution status
questions.explanation: The test basis is all the information (requirements specifications, design documents, user stories, risk analyses, etc.) used as the source for deriving test conditions and test cases.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of using a well-defined software development lifecycle model when planning testing?
options: It makes later updates to the test plan unnecessary as the project progresses
It helps show when testing should take place relative to development activities
It ensures that no defects are introduced into the code during the development work
It removes the need for a dedicated test environment on the project
questions.explanation: Understanding the lifecycle model (e.g., sequential, iterative) helps testers know when to plan, design, and execute tests relative to related development activities.

questions.question: In a DevOps context with continuous delivery, why is a high level of test automation especially important?
options: DevOps rules out manual testing altogether, so every check must be scripted in advance
DevOps removes the need for any kind of testing before a release is delivered
Fast, frequent delivery cycles need rapid feedback that manual testing can't give
Automated tests need no maintenance, which keeps the delivery pipeline cheap to run
questions.explanation: DevOps and continuous delivery rely on fast, frequent builds and releases; a strong suite of automated tests is needed to provide the rapid feedback these short cycles demand.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical test basis for component (unit) testing?
options: Business requirements and user needs documents
User acceptance criteria and business scenarios
Detailed design, code and data models
Production incident reports from live service
questions.explanation: Component testing is typically based on detailed design specifications, code itself, and data models, since it focuses on individual components in isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes 'operational acceptance testing'?
options: Testing done by end users to validate their own business processes and workflows
Testing carried out to demonstrate compliance with legal or regulatory requirements
Testing performed during component integration to check the interfaces between parts
Testing operational aspects such as backup, restore and disaster recovery
questions.explanation: Operational acceptance testing focuses on operational aspects like backup and restore, disaster recovery, user management, and maintenance tasks, usually conducted by system administrators.

questions.question: Which combination of test type and example is CORRECTLY matched?
options: Functional testing: verifying that a shopping cart total is calculated correctly
Non-functional testing: verifying that a business rule applies the correct discount
White-box testing: verifying that the system meets usability requirements
Change-related testing: verifying a brand-new feature for the first time
questions.explanation: Verifying that a specific function (calculating a total) produces correct output is a functional test example; the remaining pairs match a test type with an inappropriate example.

questions.question: Which quality characteristic would 'security testing' PRIMARILY assess?
options: Whether data and resources are protected from unauthorized access
Whether the user interface follows the corporate branding guidelines
Whether the software installs on several operating systems
Whether response times stay within target under load
questions.explanation: Security testing evaluates confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and other aspects related to protecting data and resources from unauthorized access.

questions.question: A company decides to automatically re-run a subset of tests every time code is committed. This is BEST described as:
options: Regression testing built into a continuous integration pipeline
Confirmation testing of a defect that was fixed in the most recent commit
Acceptance testing performed by business users on each of the commits
Maintenance testing following a release of the software to production
questions.explanation: Running an automated subset of tests on every commit to catch unintended side effects of changes is a form of regression testing, commonly integrated into CI pipelines.

questions.question: Which of the following work products can typically be examined using static testing techniques?
options: Executable source code in the repository
Compiled binaries produced by the build
Production log files from the live system
Requirements, user stories, code and test plans
questions.explanation: Static testing techniques such as reviews and static analysis can be applied to many types of work products, including requirements, user stories, design documents, code, and test documentation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of static testing compared to dynamic testing?
options: It can measure actual runtime performance and resource use of the running system
It finds more defects than dynamic testing does on every kind of project
It makes later dynamic testing unnecessary once the reviews have been completed
It finds defects earlier, before code can run, lowering the cost of fixing them
questions.explanation: Static testing can be performed before code exists or is executable, allowing defects in requirements or design to be found and fixed earlier and more cheaply than if found later via dynamic testing.

questions.question: During the 'individual review' (preparation) activity of a formal review, participants primarily:
options: Examining the work product alone beforehand, noting defects and questions
Meeting as a group to discuss the work product and to log all of the defects found
Signing off the work product as approved so that it can move to the next phase
Applying fixes to the defects that the other participants have already found
questions.explanation: In individual review (preparation), each participant examines the work product on their own before any review meeting, identifying potential defects, questions, and comments to bring to the meeting.

questions.question: In a formal review, which role is typically responsible for the work product being reviewed and for fixing identified defects?
options: The moderator
The reviewer
The manager
The author
questions.explanation: The author created the work product under review and is generally responsible for addressing (fixing) the defects found.

questions.question: A 'walkthrough' review type is generally characterized by:
options: The author leads the session, often to build consensus or educate, informally
A formal process with strict entry and exit criteria, led by a trained moderator
The author stays out of the session so that reviewers can speak freely
Tool-driven analysis of the work product with no human participants
questions.explanation: A walkthrough is typically led by the author, aiming to gather feedback, build consensus, or educate participants; it is usually less formal than an inspection.

questions.question: Which factor is generally considered when deciding how formal a review should be for a given work product?
options: The number of participants who happen to be available on the day of the review
Whether the moderator happens to prefer formal meetings over informal discussions
The programming language and framework used by the development team in the project
Process maturity, criticality of the work product, and regulatory requirements
questions.explanation: Review formality is usually chosen based on factors such as the lifecycle model, process maturity, criticality of the work product, legal/regulatory requirements, and time/budget constraints.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST supports a blame-free review culture that helps reviews succeed?
options: Ranking authors publicly according to how many defects were found in their work
Having authors justify every single comment in front of the management team
Giving authors no feedback at all so that they are never made to feel criticized
Focusing feedback on the work product, not the person, and valuing the defects found
questions.explanation: A successful review culture treats found defects as valuable contributions to improving the work product, focusing objectively on the artifact rather than criticizing the author personally.

questions.question: A requirements document states 'the system shall respond quickly to user requests.' Which type of defect would a static review MOST likely flag here?
options: A performance defect that only load testing could ever manage to reveal
A security vulnerability in the way the system handles incoming requests
A regression defect that was introduced by a recent change to the code
An ambiguity, since 'quickly' is not measurable or testable as written
questions.explanation: Static testing is effective at catching ambiguous or untestable requirements, such as a vague, unmeasurable term like 'quickly', before any code is written.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes the 'manager' role's typical responsibility in a formal review?
options: Recording the defects and open points raised during the review meeting itself
Fixing all of the defects that were identified by the reviewers afterwards
Deciding which reviews occur, allocating resources, checking objectives are met
Leading the review meeting and moderating the discussion between participants
questions.explanation: The manager typically decides what gets reviewed, allocates time and resources for reviews within project schedules, and evaluates whether review objectives are being achieved.

questions.question: Static analysis tools are commonly used to detect which of the following in source code, WITHOUT executing it?
options: Unreachable code, undeclared variables and breaches of coding standards
Memory usage while the system is running at peak load in the test environment
How satisfied the end users are with the interface they have been given
Response times of particular business transactions while the system is running
questions.explanation: Static analysis tools examine code structure without executing it, commonly detecting issues like unreachable code, unused variables, and coding standard violations.

questions.question: What typically happens during the 'follow-up' activity at the end of a formal review process?
options: Nothing further, since the review is considered finished once the meeting has ended
Checking that defects were dealt with and gathering metrics on the review itself
Scheduling the kick-off meeting for the next review of the following work product
Sending the work product to the reviewers for the first time so they can start
questions.explanation: Follow-up confirms that defects have been appropriately addressed (fixed, deferred, or rejected with reason) and gathers metrics to check whether exit criteria are met and to improve future reviews.

questions.question: Which statement CORRECTLY differentiates black-box, white-box, and experience-based test techniques?
options: Black-box techniques use internal code structure, while white-box techniques use only specifications
Black-box uses specifications, white-box uses structure, experience-based uses tester knowledge
The three categories are functionally the same and differ only in name
Experience-based techniques can be applied to non-functional testing alone
questions.explanation: Black-box techniques are specification-based, white-box techniques are structure-based, and experience-based techniques leverage the tester's skill, intuition, and experience with similar systems or defects.

questions.question: A password field must be between 8 and 20 characters. Using boundary value analysis with two-point boundaries, which values should be tested for the MINIMUM boundary?
options: 8 and 9
7 and 8
1 and 8
19 and 20
questions.explanation: Two-point boundary value analysis for a minimum boundary of 8 tests the invalid value just below it (7) and the valid minimum itself (8).

questions.question: A discount system applies: 0% for orders under $50, 10% for orders from $50 to $199.99, and 20% for orders of $200 or more. Using equivalence partitioning, how many valid partitions exist for the order amount?
questions.explanation: There are three valid discount partitions based on the order amount: under $50, $50-$199.99, and $200 or more, each producing a distinct discount behavior.

questions.question: A decision table combines conditions 'Has valid coupon' (Y/N) and 'Order total >= $50' (Y/N), yielding 4 rules with distinct actions. If two test cases only cover 2 of the 4 rules, what decision table coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Decision table coverage = (rules exercised / total rules) x 100%. Covering 2 out of 4 rules yields 50% decision table coverage.

questions.question: A state model has 4 states and 6 valid transitions. A test suite visits all 4 states but exercises only 3 of the valid transitions. What valid-transition coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Valid-transition coverage is the number of valid transitions exercised divided by the total number of valid transitions: 3 of 6 is 50%, even though every state was visited.

questions.question: Which of the following is a KEY advantage of boundary value analysis over simple equivalence partitioning?
options: It needs fewer test cases than equivalence partitioning in every situation
It targets range edges, where off-by-one defects are more likely to occur
It removes the need to analyze the specification
It applies to non-functional testing alone
questions.explanation: Boundary value analysis complements equivalence partitioning by focusing specifically on boundary values, where off-by-one and similar errors are empirically more common.

questions.question: Why is 100% statement coverage generally considered a stronger criterion than merely running a few 'happy path' test cases, but still not sufficient on its own?
options: Each statement ran at least once, but some decision outcomes may still be untested
Every possible combination of inputs has been exercised by the tests that were run
It always takes more test cases than decision coverage does to reach full coverage
It can be applied to non-functional testing alone and not to functional behavior
questions.explanation: 100% statement coverage confirms every statement executed at least once, but a decision with two branches might still only be tested with one outcome, leaving decision logic under-tested.

questions.question: Which of the following would typically be included in a test strategy rather than a project-specific test plan?
options: The schedule for test execution during one particular sprint of a single project
The list of defects that were logged during one specific test cycle
The names of the testers who were assigned to one particular release
The generic organization-wide approach to testing across several projects
questions.explanation: A test strategy is typically a high-level, organization- or program-wide description of the general test approach, while a test plan addresses the specifics of a given project or level.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an 'analytical' test strategy?
options: A risk-based approach, prioritizing effort by likelihood and impact of product risks
Testing guided purely by the tester's intuition, with no prior analysis of any kind
Reusing test cases from an earlier, unrelated project without any adaptation to this one
Choosing test cases at random, with no regard for requirements or for risk
questions.explanation: Analytical strategies, such as risk-based testing, systematically analyze some basis (e.g., requirements or risks) to determine and prioritize test conditions and test cases.

questions.question: During risk-based testing, a high-likelihood, high-impact product risk should generally result in:
options: Lighter testing, in order to save time for other areas
More thorough testing, carried out earlier, in that risk area
No testing, because testing cannot lower risk
Postponing testing until after release
questions.explanation: In risk-based testing, areas with higher risk levels (combining likelihood and impact) are typically tested more thoroughly and earlier to reduce the residual risk before release.

questions.question: Which activity is part of the ongoing risk management process throughout a project, not just a one-time activity?
options: Risks are assessed once at the start and the resulting assessment is then left unchanged
New risks can be identified by the test manager acting alone on the project
Risk identification, analysis and mitigation are revisited as the project evolves
Product risks and project risks are assessed against exactly the same criteria
questions.explanation: Risk management is iterative: new risks can emerge and existing risk assessments may need updating throughout the project as more information becomes available.

questions.question: Which of the following metrics would be MOST useful for monitoring test progress during test execution?
options: The number of employees who currently work for the company as a whole
The colors that were chosen for the dashboard of the test management tool
Test cases run, passed, failed and blocked, compared with the planned total
The number of breaks that the members of the test team take each day
questions.explanation: Common test progress metrics include the percentage of planned test cases executed and their pass/fail/blocked status, which help monitor whether testing is on track against exit criteria.

questions.question: If test monitoring reveals that test execution is significantly behind schedule, which test CONTROL action might a test manager take?
options: Carrying on exactly as planned and simply ignoring the delay that has been observed
Re-prioritizing tests by risk so critical areas run first in the remaining time
Cancelling the whole test phase straight away without consulting any stakeholders
Adding a large number of low-priority test cases to make up the lost time
questions.explanation: Test control involves taking corrective actions based on monitoring information, such as re-prioritizing tests by risk when time is constrained, to ensure the most important tests are still executed.

questions.question: Which piece of information in a defect report helps a developer decide HOW URGENTLY to fix it, as opposed to how severe the technical impact is?
options: Severity
The tester's name
Priority
The operating system version of the test environment
questions.explanation: Priority indicates the urgency or order in which a defect should be fixed relative to others, while severity reflects the technical/business impact of the defect itself; the two can differ.

questions.question: Which of the following would typically be an EXIT criterion for a system test level?
options: All planned tests have run and an agreed share of critical defects is fixed
At least one developer has glanced over the code of the system under test
The project manager has approved the initial budget for the test effort
The test environment has been requested but has not yet been set up
questions.explanation: Typical exit criteria include completion of planned test execution and resolution/verification of an agreed proportion of defects (often weighted by severity), among other measurable conditions.

questions.question: Which factor would MOST directly increase the 'impact' component of a product risk (assuming likelihood stays constant)?
options: The feature is used by a small handful of internal testers and by nobody else
The feature is critical to many paying customers and central to revenue
The feature is scheduled to be removed from the product in the next release
The feature already has extensive documentation covering its intended behavior
questions.explanation: Impact reflects the consequences of a risk materializing; a widely used, revenue-critical feature failing has a much higher business impact than an obscure or soon-to-be-removed one.

questions.question: Which of the following is generally the PRIMARY purpose of a test summary report?
options: Assigning blame to individuals for the defects that were found late in the project
Taking the place of the test plan on all of the organization's future projects
Listing the pay and other employment details of each of the testers
Giving stakeholders a summary of testing done, results, and quality and residual risk
questions.explanation: A test summary report communicates to stakeholders a summary of testing activities and results, along with an evaluation of quality and any outstanding risks, typically at the end of a test level or phase.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST illustrates using a risk-based approach to determine test TECHNIQUES (not just priority)?
options: Applying one and the same technique to every feature, regardless of its level of risk
Skipping test design for high-risk features in order to save time for execution
Giving the highest-risk feature to whichever tester has the least experience
Rigorous techniques such as decision tables for high-risk complex rules
questions.explanation: Risk-based testing can influence not just the order and depth of testing but also the choice of test techniques, applying more rigorous techniques where risk is higher.

questions.question: Which of the following is a potential BENEFIT of using test management tools?
options: They improve traceability between requirements, tests and defects
They remove the need for testers altogether once the tool has been configured
They deliver full coverage of the requirements without any further effort from the team
They eliminate all of the risk from the project once they are in use
questions.explanation: Test management tools support traceability (linking requirements to tests and defects) and provide reporting/monitoring capabilities that help manage test progress, though they don't guarantee coverage or eliminate risk.

questions.question: Which category of tool would be used to support static testing by automatically checking source code against coding standards?
options: Performance testing tools
Test data preparation tools
Test execution tools
Static analysis tools
questions.explanation: Static analysis tools examine code (or other artifacts) without executing it, commonly used to check adherence to coding standards, calculate metrics, and detect certain classes of defects.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a test data preparation tool?
options: To generate or extract test data, such as production data with fields masked
To write complete test cases from scratch with no human input of any kind
To measure the performance of the system under test while it is under load
To take the place of a requirements management tool within the test process
questions.explanation: Test data preparation tools help create, extract, subset, or anonymize data (e.g. masking sensitive fields from production data) for use as realistic test inputs.

questions.question: A 'test comparator' tool is used to:
options: Comparing the productivity of two different testers over a period of several weeks
Comparing the costs of two different test management tools offered by vendors
Comparing the hardware specifications of two different test environments in use
Comparing actual results of the test object with expected results
questions.explanation: Test comparators automatically compare actual outcomes (e.g. output files, screen content, or database state) with expected results, often used within test execution tools.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes a benefit of test tool support in general?
options: Removing the need for skilled testers from the project once the tools are in place
Making the software free of defects as soon as the automated tests are running
Cutting repetitive manual work such as rerunning regression tests
Guaranteeing that the licence costs of the tools are kept at zero for the project
questions.explanation: Tool support can automate repetitive tasks like regression test execution, improving consistency and repeatability and freeing testers for more exploratory or analytical work.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common LIMITATION or risk of test automation, even with a good tool?
options: Automated tests run faster than manual tests in every case, whatever they check
Automated tests need no maintenance once they have been written and committed
Automated checks that merely repeat can give false confidence over time
Automated tests are able to fully replace exploratory testing in the project
questions.explanation: Automated regression suites can suffer from the pesticide paradox too — repeatedly running the same automated checks may stop finding new defects unless the suite is reviewed and evolved.

questions.question: Which type of tool is specifically designed to simulate a large number of concurrent virtual users to assess system behavior under load?
options: Performance/load testing tool
Requirements management tool
Static analysis tool
Coverage measurement tool
questions.explanation: Performance (load) testing tools simulate many concurrent virtual users or transactions to evaluate response times, throughput, and resource usage under expected or peak load.

questions.question: A 'code coverage tool' is primarily used to:
options: Measuring which statements or branches of the code the tests exercised
Writing the new source code for a feature automatically from its requirements
Predicting how many defects will be found in production after the release
Managing the budget and the schedule of the whole project for the sponsors
questions.explanation: Code coverage tools instrument or analyze code execution to report which statements, branches, or other structural elements were exercised during test execution.

questions.question: Before selecting a test automation tool for an organization, which of the following is a RECOMMENDED first step?
options: Buy the most expensive tool on the assumption that it fits best
Assess needs, constraints and process maturity, and consider a proof of concept
Let each team pick its own tool with no coordination
Automate all existing manual test cases straight away, whether suitable or not
questions.explanation: Best practice is to assess organizational needs, evaluate the current test process, and run a proof-of-concept with one or more candidate tools before committing to a tool across the organization.

questions.question: Which tool category would most directly help manage and track defect reports throughout their lifecycle (new, open, fixed, closed)?
options: Static analysis tool
Performance testing tool
Defect management tool
Test data preparation tool
questions.explanation: Defect (incident) management tools support logging, tracking, and managing the workflow status of defect reports from creation through resolution and closure.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common SUCCESS FACTOR for tool introduction in an organization?
options: Rolling the tool out across the whole organization at once, with no pilot stage
Skipping training altogether on the grounds that the tool should be intuitive
Choosing the tool without consulting the people who will have to use it
Piloting on a small project, giving training and setting usage guidelines first
questions.explanation: Success factors for tool adoption include piloting on a pilot project, providing appropriate training and coaching, and defining clear usage guidelines before rolling the tool out more broadly.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a tool that supports MANAGEMENT of testing and test activities, rather than test execution itself?
options: A GUI test execution tool that replays user actions recorded earlier in the session
A performance monitoring tool that measures response times of live transactions
A requirements management tool used to trace requirements to test cases
A code coverage tool that instruments the source code of the system under test
questions.explanation: Requirements management tools (and similar tools like test management tools) support the management of testing, such as traceability, planning, and reporting, distinct from tools that execute or analyze tests directly.

questions.question: Which statement about record-and-playback test execution tools is MOST accurate?
options: Recorded scripts need no maintenance, however much the user interface is changed
They produce meaningful assertions on their own, without any input from the tester
They can be used for performance testing alone and not for functional testing
They create tests quickly, but scripts often need heavy maintenance after UI changes
questions.explanation: Record-and-playback tools can quickly generate scripts by capturing user actions, but the resulting scripts are often brittle and need considerable maintenance whenever the UI changes.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about test tools is CORRECT?
options: Each tool category performs one function with no overlap
Some tools combine several functions, such as test management with defect tracking
Test tools are useful to large organizations alone
A tool, once bought, never needs to be re-evaluated
questions.explanation: Many commercial and open-source tools combine multiple capabilities (e.g. test management plus defect tracking and reporting) rather than strictly fitting into a single narrow category.
